curves.title: Global average temperature
curves.note: Worked out by combining more than 150,000 chemical temperature readings from fossil shells and ancient sea-floor mud with climate-model runs, one value per geological stage; the broad ups and downs are well supported, but any single value is uncertain by several degrees (the band is the 5th to 95th percentile).

source.title: PhanDA: files with the GMST, CO2 and LTG values of Judd et al. (2024), A 485-million-year history of Earth's surface temperature, Science 385, eadk3705
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (repository LICENSE file: 'Attribution 4.0 International'; README badge 'License: CC BY 4.0')

curves.how: File 5_Outputs/PhanDA_GMSTandCO2_percentiles.csv, all 85 stage rows (Tremadocian, base 486.85 Ma, to Holocene). x = AverageAge (midpoint of the stage, Ma), y = GMST_50 (median), band = GMST_05 to GMST_95. Rounded to 0.1 °C; no resampling or smoothing. Each value is a stage average, so events shorter than a stage (for example the 200,000-year warm spike 56 million years ago) do not show.

curves.title: Carbon dioxide in the air
curves.note: Estimated from chemical and fossil clues such as the pores on fossil leaves, ancient soils and boron in sea shells, averaged over each geological stage; values for the last 66 million years are fairly firm, older ones are rough and the Mesozoic is the least certain (the band is the 5th to 95th percentile).

source.title: PhanDA: files with the GMST, CO2 and LTG values of Judd et al. (2024), A 485-million-year history of Earth's surface temperature, Science 385, eadk3705. Its CO2 series is 'largely based on the data from Foster et al. (2017) in the Paleozoic and Mesozoic, and the data from Rae et al. (2021) in the Cenozoic' (Judd et al. 2024, Fig. 4 caption)
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (repository LICENSE file: 'Attribution 4.0 International'; README badge 'License: CC BY 4.0')

curves.how: Same file and rows as the temperature curve. x = AverageAge, y = CO2_50 (median), band = CO2_05 to CO2_95, rounded to 1 ppm; no resampling. The youngest row (Holocene, 276 ppm) is the pre-industrial level, not today's (over 420 ppm).

curves.title: Carbon dioxide in the air (finer curve, older study)
curves.note: A smooth line fitted through more than 1,200 separate CO2 estimates made by five different methods (fossil leaves, ancient soils, sea-shell chemistry and others); it shows the long swings in CO2 well, but newer work puts CO2 around 55 to 45 million years ago clearly higher than this line does.

source.title: Foster, G. L., Royer, D. L. & Lunt, D. J. (2017) Future climate forcing potentially without precedent in the last 420 million years. Nature Communications 8, 14845. Supplementary Data 2 (LOESS fit)
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (article page: 'This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License')

curves.how: Supplementary Data 2 (file 41467_2017_BFncomms14845_MOESM2875_ESM.xlsx, sheet 'LOESS Fit', 840 rows at 0.5 Myr steps). x = 'Age (Ma)', y = 'pCO2 probability maximum', band = 'lw68%' to 'up68%'. Thinned, not smoothed: every row from 0 to 66 Ma, every fourth row (2 Myr steps) before that. Do not join this line to the 'co2' curve: they are two different reconstructions.

curves.title: Oxygen in the air
curves.note: A consensus curve: the authors weighed the different ways of estimating ancient oxygen against each other and drew the most likely path between them; it is a best judgement, not a measurement, and the band shows how far the methods disagree (often by ten percentage points or more).

source.title: Mills, B. J. W., Krause, A. J., Jarvis, I. & Cramer, B. D. (2023) Evolution of Atmospheric O2 Through the Phanerozoic, Revisited. Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences 51, 253-276. Data of Figure 6
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 for the article (Crossref licence record for the DOI: http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The author's GitHub data repository ('Data from Figure 6 in Mills et al. (2023)') carries no separate licence file.

curves.how: File Mills_etal_2023_AREPS_O2.xlsx, Sheet1, 542 rows at 1 Myr steps (columns Time, Mid, Min, Max; Time is negative Ma). x = -Time, y = Mid, band = Min to Max, in percent of the atmosphere. Thinned to every second row (odd ages 541 to 1 Ma, plus 0); rounded to 0.1; no smoothing.

curves.title: Oxygen in the air before animals (rough limits)
curves.note: Only upper and lower limits are known, from chemical traces in very old rocks: almost no free oxygen before about 2.4 billion years ago, then somewhere between a ten-thousandth and a tenth of today's level for more than a billion years, rising towards modern levels after about 800 million years ago; the limits span factors of a thousand or more and are still argued over.

source.title: Ranges as stated in Chen, G. et al. (2022) Reconstructing Earth's atmospheric oxygenation history using machine learning, Nature Communications 13, 5862 (introduction and methods, summarising the two-step model of Lyons et al. 2014); checked against Kasting & Ji (2025), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, doi 10.1098/rstb.2024.0093, and Lyons et al. (2021), Astrobiology 21, 906, doi 10.1089/ast.2020.2418 (both CC BY 4.0)
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (article page: 'licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License')

curves.how: Not a data file: six range points built from numbers stated in the text of the paper. 'from 10^-9 to 10^-5 PAL pre-GOE' (4000 to 2500 Ma); the Great Oxidation Event 'around 2.5 to 2.0 billion years ago'; '10^-4 to 10^-1 PAL during the boring billion interval from ~2.0 to 1.0 Ga' (held to 800 Ma, where Lyons et al. 2021 put the start of the second rise, 'between 800 and 600 million years ago'); '10^-1 to ~1 PAL from ~0.5 Ga to present' (placed at 541 Ma, the start of the Phanerozoic curve). PAL (present atmospheric level) converted to percent of the air by multiplying by 20.95. The straight lines between the points are schematic; use a logarithmic axis. Points are [Ma, low, high].

curves.title: Global sea level
curves.note: Worked out by measuring, on maps of ancient coastlines drawn every 10 million years, how much of today's land was under the sea, then converting flooded area into a height; it shows the big long swings but the heights are uncertain by many tens of metres and other methods give lower values, especially before 250 million years ago.

source.title: Marcilly, C. M., Torsvik, T. H. & Conrad, C. P. (2022) Global Phanerozoic sea levels from paleogeographic flooding maps. Gondwana Research 110, 128-142. Table 1
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (first page of the article: 'This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)')

curves.how: Table 1 of the article PDF (open copy from the Norwegian research archive), all 53 rows, 520 to 0 Ma at 10 Myr steps. x = 'Age (Ma)', y = column 'Modern land sea level (C = 0.0057 km/10^6 km2), relative m', rounded to 1 m; no resampling. Text extracted with pdftotext; the PDF's minus glyph was restored by hand-checked rule (this column is negative only at 30 Ma, -2.88 m, and 10 Ma, -3.62 m). Ten-million-year steps cannot show ice-age swings of about 120 m.

curves.title: Variety of sea animals (number of genera)
curves.note: A count of the kinds (genera) of sea animals known as fossils from each geological stage, from the Paleobiology Database; the sharp drops are the mass extinctions, but the count depends on how much rock of each age has been searched, and the fall over the last 12 million years or so is not real: the database holds fossils only, so living genera with no recent fossils drop out.

source.title: The Paleobiology Database, data service 1.2, diversity of marine Metazoa by stage (downloaded 21 November 2026)
source.licence: CC0 (response header: 'Data License: Creative Commons CC0', https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/)

curves.how: One API call (occs/diversity, base_name=Metazoa, envtype=marine, count=genera, time_reso=stage; 1,092,300 occurrences, 98 stages). y = X_Ft + X_bL + X_FL + X_bt, i.e. every genus known or implied to have lived during the stage (range-through count, raw, not corrected for sampling); x = midpoint of the stage. No resampling. The Pridoli (423 to 420 Ma) has no stage in the database and is missing. Stage dates are the database's own.

curves.title: Length of the day
curves.note: Read from regular layers in ancient sediments that record the wobble of the Earth's axis, whose pace depends on how fast the Earth spins and how far away the Moon is; ten rock sections give ten points, each good to about a quarter to half an hour, and the day may not have lengthened as smoothly between them as a joined-up line suggests.

source.title: Zhou, M., Wu, H., Hinnov, L. A., Fang, Q., Zhang, S., Yang, T. & Shi, M. (2022) Empirical reconstruction of Earth-Moon and Solar System dynamical parameters for the past 2.5 billion years from cyclostratigraphy. Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL098304. Supporting Information, Table S4
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (figshare record of the Supporting Information: licence 'CC BY 4.0')

curves.how: Table S4 of 'Supporting Informtion S1.docx' (figshare file 36699174), column 'Length of Day [h]', one point per rock section: Dales Gorge (~2465 Ma), Xiamaling (~1400), Datangpo (~655), Luoyixi (~500), Alum Shale (~493), Pingliang (~455), Wanhe (~445), Lucaogou (~269), Wujiaping (~259), Walvis Ridge (~55). Band = the table's plus-or-minus (two standard deviations for the TimeOpt MCMC rows). Lucaogou has two rows; the TimeOpt MCMC one (22.41 h) is used, the other method gives 22.78 h. The present day (0 Ma, 24.0 h) is added by hand and is not in the table. Ages are approximate ('~' in the table).

curves.title: Deep-sea climate record (oxygen isotopes)
curves.note: Measured directly in the shells of tiny sea-floor animals from drill cores, dated by counting the Earth's orbital cycles; it is the most detailed climate record of the last 66 million years, but it is a chemical signal that mixes deep-sea temperature and the amount of ice on land, not a temperature in degrees.

source.title: Westerhold, T. (2020) S34. Binned and LOESS smoothed Cenozoic deep-sea benthic foraminifer stable carbon and oxygen isotope reference splice (CENOGRID). PANGAEA. Data of Westerhold et al. (2020), Science 369, 1383-1387
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (file header: 'License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY-4.0)')

curves.how: Tab-delimited file of PANGAEA dataset 917717 (23,629 rows). x = 'Tuned time [Ma]', y = column 'ISOBENd18oLOESSsmooth' (the authors' short LOESS smooth of benthic δ18O). Thinned, not re-smoothed, by taking the nearest row to a target grid: every 0.02 Myr from 0 to 2.6 Ma, every 0.1 Myr to 10 Ma, every 0.3 Myr to 67.1 Ma. Draw with the axis upside down (warm at the top). Extra curve, not a temperature: no conversion to degrees was applied.
